astra.title: Astra
astra.short: A LangGraph agent that decides on its own when to search internal documents, call tools or just answer, inside strict security boundaries.
astra.lead: Astra is the backend of an enterprise AI assistant. An LLM agent decides on its own whether it needs internal documents (RAG over PostgreSQL + pgvector), live system tools, both, or neither, and every step runs inside security boundaries. I designed and built it end to end; the focus is the engineering around the model: orchestration, retrieval, security, failure handling, observability, testing and delivery.

sections.p: The token is checked and the user's role is loaded from the database. The agent gets only the tools that role may use, and a knowledge base tool limited to the documents this user may read. The input guardrail rejects oversized, hidden-character or prompt-injection input in English and Persian. Every tool call goes through one ToolExecutor: allow-list, role check, schema validation and retry for transient errors. The answer is redacted for secrets and returned with the route taken, the tools used and the sources.

sections.h: The agent as a state machine
sections.p: The agent is a LangGraph graph: the model node thinks and calls tools, the tools node runs them, and the result goes back to the model. A timeout or connection error goes to a recovery node instead of crashing the run. Sensitive tools, such as removing a document from the knowledge base, pause the graph with interrupt(); the state is checkpointed in PostgreSQL, so an admin can approve or reject later, even from another process.

sections.h: Agentic RAG: retrieval is a tool
sections.p: Search is not glued to every question. The model calls search_knowledge_base only when it needs internal knowledge, so general questions skip the embedding call and the extra context tokens. Documents are chunked with overlap, embedded with text-embedding-3-small and searched by cosine distance on an HNSW index, then reranked by keywords and filtered by a score threshold. Permissions are applied before retrieval, not after: private chunks never reach the model, even if an injection asks for them. Because the model can pick the wrong route, route accuracy is part of the evaluation.

No single check is trusted. Authentication, rate limits, the input guardrail, per-role tool permissions, human approval and output redaction each stop a different kind of failure. Security errors fail closed: an unknown tool or invalid arguments stop the run instead of being retried.

407 unit, integration and end-to-end tests run against a real pgvector database; only the external providers are faked. An evaluation harness measures Recall@k, MRR, route accuracy, groundedness and citation rate, and CI runs it as a regression gate next to the coverage gate. Metrics, token usage and estimated cost are exported to Prometheus, and an MCP server written against the specification exposes the read-only tools.

Rate limits, metrics and conversation memory live in process memory, so several workers would need Redis. The reranker is a simple keyword baseline. The injection check matches patterns and is only one layer. The evaluation metrics are lexical heuristics on a small dataset: they catch regressions, they are not a quality claim.

notes.title: AI Medical Notes
notes.short: Turns a doctor's consultation notes into a visit summary, next steps and an email to the patient, streamed in real time.
notes.lead: Writing up a visit takes time: a summary for the record, the next steps, and a clear message for the patient. In AI Medical Notes the doctor writes the consultation notes once, and the app streams all three back in real time. It is a complete SaaS: sign-in, a paid subscription plan, a protected product page and a serverless backend.

sections.p: The doctor signs in and opens the product page, which requires the premium plan. The form sends the patient's name, the visit date and the notes to the API with the Clerk token. FastAPI, running as a serverless function on Vercel, verifies the token, builds the prompt and streams the model's answer. The browser receives it as Server-Sent Events and renders the Markdown as it arrives, so the doctor starts reading as soon as the first words arrive instead of waiting for the whole text.

The same notes become three texts for three readers: a visit summary for the doctor's records, the next steps for the doctor, and a draft email that explains the visit to the patient in plain Persian.

Authentication and subscriptions are handled by Clerk. The backend never trusts the browser: it verifies the token's signature against Clerk's public keys on every request, and only users on the paid plan can open the product page.

price.title: Price Estimate
price.short: Predicts what a product costs from its text description, then uses that estimate inside a team of agents that hunts for online deals sold well below their real value.
price.lead: Can a model tell what a product is worth just by reading its description? Price Estimate answers that question across the whole machine learning lifecycle: building a dataset of about 800,000 Amazon products, comparing classic models, deep learning and large language models, fine-tuning an open-source LLM, blending the best models into one estimate, and finally putting that estimate to work inside a team of agents that finds deals selling well below their true value.
stats: average error of my small neural network

sections.h: From raw data to one estimate
sections.p: Products priced between $0.50 and $999 are parsed, cleaned of part numbers and noise, and deduplicated. The data is resampled so expensive items are not drowned out by cheap ones, and a small LLM rewrites every description into the same short five-line format. Three strong models then price each item: a deep residual neural network trained on log prices, a Llama 3.2 3B model fine-tuned with QLoRA and served on a GPU, and a large LLM that sees five similar products and their prices from a Chroma vector store (RAG). Their answers are blended into one estimate, served by a REST API and used by the agents.

sections.h: A ladder of models, measured honestly
sections.p: Every model prices the same 200 test items, from a constant guess up to a neural network. The chart shows the mean absolute error in dollars, so a shorter bar is better. The words of the description matter far more than size and weight. Random forest and XGBoost overlap within their confidence intervals, so neither is a clear winner on 200 items. The small neural network ties the random forest on average error but has the best hit rate, and its validation error was still falling, so it is under-trained. Each result is reported with a 95% confidence interval and several metrics, because one number can hide large errors on cheap items.

Instead of picking weights by hand, the ensemble learns them from validation predictions with non-negative least squares. If one member fails at prediction time, for example when an API is down or the GPU service is still starting, the ensemble drops it and re-weights the others instead of failing the whole estimate.

A scanner agent reads deal RSS feeds and uses an LLM with structured output to pick the deals with the clearest descriptions. The planner asks the ensemble for each deal's real value, picks the biggest discount, and if it beats a threshold the messenger sends a push notification. A memory file keeps deals already surfaced so they are not sent twice. In a second, autonomous mode the LLM itself decides which tools to call, with a turn limit and tool errors returned to the model.

Everything lives in one installable, tested Python package instead of notebooks: settings from .env, learned ensemble weights, normalization constants saved inside the neural network checkpoint so a retrained model never gives silently wrong prices, fixes for bugs that crashed the parser and the file upload, a FastAPI /predict endpoint, a pricing tab in the Gradio dashboard, my own QLoRA training script with Hugging Face TRL, and an offline test suite with fakes for every LLM and API, checked by ruff and GitHub Actions.

behengam.title: Behengam
behengam.short: Connects 12 roles of Iran's health system around one shared patient record, with an AI layer that gathers and standardizes lab results and shows trends and alerts.
behengam.lead: Behengam is an integrated health platform for Iran's health system that I founded. It connects 12 roles around one shared patient record, and each role sees the record only as far as its need and access level allow. Its tagline: health in the moment; every role of the health system, coordinated around one page.

sections.p: It started as an AI assistant for doctors. A patient's lab results are scattered across paper sheets, lab websites and photos in messengers; much of a short visit goes into putting them together; doctors cannot easily see how markers relate to each other or to medications; and early warning signs get lost among dozens of numbers. Behengam gathers the results from every lab, standardizes them (LOINC for test codes, UCUM for units) and shows trends and alerts, and it widens the idea from a doctor's tool to a network of 12 roles.

Actions in one role really show up in the others. A prescription written by the doctor reaches the patient, the chosen pharmacy and the insurer; a lab result reaches the patient, the requesting doctor and the insurer.

The doctor's interface changes with the workplace (office, hospital, clinic or university) and the visit type. It has patient intake, a patient summary with current and stopped medications and AI alerts, medical records with linked filters and a body map, AI-selected charts (a marker over time, marker against marker, marker against medication, and a forecast with a confidence band), a diagnosis desk with a chat assistant that draws the requested chart, and orders with the insurance share calculated.

Version 2 of the demo, built for investors, covers all 12 roles with dark mode, an interactive body-map filter and eight entirely fictional sample patients. It is front-end only: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with hand-made SVG charts, a Persian right-to-left interface with the Persian calendar, and browser storage shared between roles. The AI is simulated with simple methods (linear regression and rules) on the patient's own data; no real AI service is called.

Lab results arrive through HL7 v2 and FHIR adapters into Kafka; an ETL layer validates them, normalizes units with UCUM, maps tests to LOINC and matches patient identities; data is stored in PostgreSQL behind a Django REST backend for authentication, roles and permissions; and a medical AI layer adds alerts, dose-effect prediction, chart interpretation and chat, always shown to the doctor as a suggestion, never as a decision. Data-level access control, patient consent, encryption and an immutable audit log are requirements; integration with national health and insurance systems is the main risk.

site.title: This website
site.short: A digital twin, a job fit checker and a team of seven AI trading agents, with budget caps, tests and evaluations, for about $2 to $3 a month.
site.lead: This site is a real AI engineering project and a live portfolio. It is bilingual (Persian and English) with light and dark themes. Behind it: a digital twin that answers from my own documents, a job fit checker that scores a job ad honestly, and a team of seven AI agents that trade Bitcoin at real prices with virtual money while visitors try to beat them.

sections.p: Five services run in Docker: Caddy in front for HTTPS and security headers, the Next.js site, the FastAPI API, a worker for scheduled jobs and the trading meetings, and PostgreSQL with pgvector for both data and vectors. Language models are reached through AvalAI, an OpenAI-compatible provider that can be switched with two settings. The Bitcoin price comes from Iranian exchanges (Nobitex, with Wallex as a fallback), because the server is in Iran.

My resume, FAQ and project notes are split into small chunks and stored as vectors. Each question is matched against chunks in its own language with two searches at once: vector search on pgvector and BM25 keyword search, merged with reciprocal rank fusion. The keyword search was added after measuring that the embedding model ranked Persian chunks poorly. The model answers only from the sources, the answer streams word by word with Server-Sent Events, and my picture switches between listening, thinking and answering with those events. If the answer is not in the sources, the twin says so and asks for an email instead of guessing.

The model reads my whole profile, lists the requirements of the ad and marks each one met, partial or missing. Only then is the score set, and its band is enforced in code from the share of must-have skills I have, so the model cannot flatter or punish at will. Years of experience never lower the score but always show up as gaps. The temperature is 0, so the same ad gets the same score.

Seven agents meet once per trading day in a fixed order as a LangGraph graph. Prices and indicators are calculated in Python, never by the model. The risk rules live in code, not in the prompt: at most 20% of the portfolio in Bitcoin, one trade a day, a stop loss between 1% and 5%, and HOLD whenever the model's output is invalid. A meeting runs only when the first visitor of the day clicks start, so days without visitors cost nothing. Each line is saved and translated to Persian the moment it is spoken, so the first visitor watches live and everyone else sees the replay.

Every model call is checked against monthly and daily budget caps before it is made, and its real cost is recorded. Each visitor has daily limits, and when a cap is reached the site stays up with a friendly message. Cheap models were chosen after real measurements, so the whole AI bill is about two to three dollars a month.

187 backend tests run against a real PostgreSQL database with a fake model client. Evaluations with real models check the digital twin (68 of 68 questions, including refusals and prompt injections), the job fit checker (9 of 9 ads) and the trading team (20 of 20 meetings with no broken risk rule).
